justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for the S&P 500 across all three horizons, anchored around the 3,071–3,110 range. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is driven primarily by recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies in the short run, assuming no major overnight catalysts. The slight upward drift in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a baseline assumption that equity markets tend to grind higher over time in the absence of recessionary shocks, combined with any prevailing monetary policy backdrop that may be supportive of risk assets. The relatively modest appreciation built into the one-month estimate acknowledges that valuations and macro headwinds constrain aggressive upside.

The confidence interval widths widen meaningfully as the horizon extends, which is standard given how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, intraday and overnight volatility are relatively bounded, so the 90% interval spans roughly 120 points. By one week, macro data releases, Federal Reserve communications, and geopolitical developments can introduce larger swings, widening the band to about 250 points. At one month, earnings reports, inflation prints, central bank decisions, and shifts in investor sentiment all add layers of uncertainty, pushing the interval to roughly 540 points. These widths are calibrated to reflect historical realized volatility in the index rather than just implied volatility, which can sometimes overstate near-term risk.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in economic data — particularly employment or manufacturing figures — could trigger a rapid repricing of recession risk and push the index below 2,840. A sudden hawkish pivot from the Federal Reserve, credit market stress, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions (such as a major conflict or trade disruption) could amplify selling pressure beyond what the intervals capture. On the upside, a surprise dovish policy shift, a strong earnings season, or a resolution of trade or geopolitical uncertainties could drive the index above 3,380 within a month. Tail events by definition sit outside probabilistic intervals, and in equity markets they tend to cluster — meaning if one shock materializes, others often follow, making the tails fatter than a simple normal distribution would suggest.
